subject: Economics
description: Articles, Annual Financial Statement, types of expenditure, FRBM, recent reforms

questions.stem: The Indian Union Budget — formally the 'Annual Financial Statement' — is provided for under:
questions.explanation: Article 112 — President shall cause the AFS (estimated receipts + expenditure) of the Government of India for a financial year to be laid before both Houses of Parliament. Article 110 — Money Bill definition. Article 280 — Finance Commission. Article 246 — distribution of legislative powers (lists). The Finance Bill (taxation proposals) and Appropriation Bill (withdrawal authorisation) are presented alongside.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Union Budget is currently presented on:

options.option_text: Last working day of February (old tradition)
1 February (advanced from end of February since 2017)

questions.explanation: Earlier the Budget was presented on the last working day of February at 5 PM (British colonial timing). Yashwant Sinha (NDA-1) advanced timing to 11 AM IST in 1999. Arun Jaitley (Modi govt) advanced the date to 1 February starting Budget 2017-18 — to enable expenditure to start from 1 April (start of FY) without 'vote on account'. The Railway Budget (separate since 1924, Acworth Committee) was MERGED with Union Budget from 2017-18.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: FRBM Act, 2003 (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act) was enacted to:

options.option_text: Reduce fiscal deficit and ensure inter-generational equity in fiscal management

questions.explanation: FRBM Act 2003 — set targets to cap fiscal deficit (3% of GDP) and revenue deficit (zero) by 2008-09 (later extended). Mandates Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement, FRBM compliance reports. N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended replacement with FRBM 2.0 — flexible glide path with 'escape clauses' for emergencies. Fiscal deficit hit ~9.2% of GDP during COVID (FY 2020-21). Current target — 4.4% (FY 2025-26), 4.3% (FY 2026-27); aiming toward 3% by FY 2028-29.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Total Government expenditure consists of two main categories:
questions.explanation: Two-fold classification. REVENUE EXPENDITURE — recurring, doesn't create asset (salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies, defence revenue, grants to states). Largest share — typically 75-80%. CAPITAL EXPENDITURE — asset-creating (infrastructure, defence equipment, capital outlay on PSUs, loans to states). Around 20-25%. Government has been emphasising capex — FY 2025-26 capex budget ~₹11.1 lakh crore. Plan vs Non-Plan distinction was abolished in 2017 — only Revenue/Capital classification remains.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: FISCAL DEFICIT is best defined as:

options.option_text: Total expenditure − Total receipts (excluding borrowings); essentially the borrowing requirement

questions.explanation: Fiscal Deficit (FD) = Total Expenditure − (Total Receipts excluding borrowings) = Total Borrowings of the Government. This is what gets 'financed' by issuing G-Secs, raising loans, drawing down cash balance. Other deficit measures: Revenue Deficit (Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts); Primary Deficit (FD − Interest Payments); Effective Revenue Deficit (Revenue Deficit − Grants for capital asset creation, abandoned 2022). India aims for fiscal deficit < 4.5% by FY 2025-26 per FRBM trajectory.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The 'Vote on Account' permits the government to:

options.option_text: Levy new taxes for the next 6 months
Withdraw money from the Consolidated Fund of India for a part of the year (typically 2 months) before full Budget approval

questions.explanation: Vote on Account (Article 116) — interim authorisation for Government to draw from CFI (typically for 2 months — covers election period before a new government's full budget). Used in election years OR if budget is delayed. NO new taxation can be introduced. The full Annual Budget is presented later by the new government. Distinct from 'Interim Budget' which is the practice of an outgoing government presenting a brief budget before elections — typically a Vote on Account + minor tax tweaks.

questions.stem: Largest source of CENTRAL government's tax revenue (FY 2024-25) is:

options.option_text: GST + Income tax combined dominate (Income Tax slightly larger than GST)

questions.explanation: Top tax sources (FY 24-25): Income Tax (incl. corporate ~30%, personal ~25-28% of gross tax), GST (~26-28%), Customs (~7%), Excise on petroleum (~6%), Cesses/Surcharges. Personal income tax has overtaken corporate tax in recent years. Direct tax (income, corporate) ≈ 55-58% of total; indirect (GST, customs) ≈ 42-45%. Composition has shifted toward direct taxes post-GST. Non-tax revenue (RBI dividend, PSU dividends, fees) is also substantial — RBI alone gave ~₹2.1 lakh crore in 2024.
